messages.content: I want to develop a semantic parser that can tell when an utterance is genuinely ambiguous, rather than treating the model’s own uncertainty as ambiguity. This distinction needs to hold under unseen compositional structures.

The central distinction is between a property of the utterance and a property of the parser. An utterance is genuinely ambiguous when it admits more than one valid interpretation. Model uncertainty means the parser is unsure what to predict; that uncertainty alone does not establish that multiple interpretations are valid. The goal is for the parser to keep those cases separate even when it encounters compositional structures it has not seen before.
So an unfamiliar structure might make the parser hesitate without making the utterance ambiguous?

Yes. Hesitation about an unfamiliar structure could reflect difficulty interpreting it, while the utterance may still have only one valid interpretation. Conversely, an utterance can have multiple valid interpretations regardless of how confident the parser appears. Confidence and genuine ambiguity should not be treated as interchangeable.
What is the quantitative target for detecting ambiguity?

The target is ambiguity-detection F1 of at least 0.85 on unseen compositions. That target is to be assessed using independently annotated sets of valid interpretations, so the distinction is grounded in interpretations judged valid independently of the parser’s uncertainty.
Does F1 ≥0.85 mean that execution accuracy must also be at least 0.85?

No. The F1 ≥0.85 threshold applies specifically to ambiguity detection on unseen compositions. F1 combines precision and recall for that detection task; it is not the stated threshold for execution accuracy. Execution accuracy has a separate comparison target.
Why specify sets of valid interpretations instead of just asking whether the model feels uncertain?

The sets provide an independent basis for judging whether more than one interpretation is valid. A model’s uncertainty is an internal signal and can arise even when there is only one valid interpretation. Using independently annotated sets keeps the ambiguity assessment focused on the utterance rather than on the parser’s confidence.
Is the requirement that the parser reproduce every interpretation in those sets?

The stated requirement is to achieve ambiguity-detection F1 ≥0.85 on unseen compositions using those independently annotated sets. It does not specify an output format or say that reproducing every interpretation is itself a separate target. The sets establish the reference for evaluating genuine ambiguity.
And how should I describe the unambiguous-input requirement?

On unambiguous inputs, the parser should match the execution accuracy of a single-output parser trained on identical data. That comparison matters alongside ambiguity detection: distinguishing ambiguous utterances must not come at the expense of the stated execution-accuracy target for inputs with one valid interpretation.
What does the identical-data condition apply to?

It applies to the training data in the comparison. The single-output parser used as the execution-accuracy baseline is trained on identical data. The goal does not additionally specify that the two parsers must have identical architectures, outputs, or training procedures.
Is there a fixed execution-accuracy percentage to hit?

No fixed percentage is stated for that measure. The target is comparative: match the single-output parser’s execution accuracy on unambiguous inputs when that parser is trained on identical data. The numerical threshold supplied here—F1 ≥0.85—belongs to ambiguity detection on unseen compositions.
Suppose ambiguity detection reaches the F1 threshold, but execution accuracy on unambiguous inputs is below the comparison parser’s. Would that satisfy the goal?

Not fully. Both conditions are part of the goal: ambiguity-detection F1 must reach at least 0.85 on unseen compositions using independently annotated sets of valid interpretations, and unambiguous-input execution accuracy must match that of the single-output parser trained on identical data.
The reverse would also fall short, then: matching execution accuracy would not compensate for missing the ambiguity-detection target?
Correct. The execution-accuracy comparison and the ambiguity-detection threshold are separate requirements. Meeting one would not, by itself, establish that the other has been met.
When you say unseen compositional structures, should I read that as a claim that every component is unfamiliar?

No. The stated condition concerns unseen compositional structures and unseen compositions; it does not say that every component must be unfamiliar. The important point is that the ambiguity distinction must hold in the specified compositional-generalization setting, rather than only where the parser recognizes a familiar overall structure.
Could I simply label every low-confidence prediction as ambiguous to cover difficult unseen compositions?

That would collapse the very distinction the goal asks the parser to make. Low confidence might indicate model uncertainty about an utterance with only one valid interpretation. Ambiguity detection needs to concern genuinely valid alternative interpretations, as assessed against the independently annotated sets, rather than uncertainty alone.
Does this commit us to a particular way of representing uncertainty or producing interpretations?

No particular representation or implementation is specified. The goal states what the parser should distinguish and how its performance should compare: ambiguity-detection F1 ≥0.85 on unseen compositions using independently annotated sets of valid interpretations, while matching the identical-data single-output parser’s execution accuracy on unambiguous inputs.
So the F1 result and the execution-accuracy comparison refer to different input conditions?

Yes. The ambiguity-detection threshold is explicitly for unseen compositions. The execution-accuracy comparison is explicitly for unambiguous inputs. Those conditions should be kept attached to their respective requirements rather than folded into one undifferentiated performance claim.
Can you put the aim in one compact statement without losing either condition?

Develop a semantic parser that distinguishes genuine utterance ambiguity from model uncertainty under unseen compositional structures, achieves ambiguity-detection F1 ≥0.85 on unseen compositions using independently annotated sets of valid interpretations, and matches the unambiguous-input execution accuracy of a single-output parser trained on identical data.

For the parser design, I propose keeping a single-output execution backbone and adding an ambiguity flag. The flag should be raised only when grammar-constrained, paraphrase-stable alternatives pass calibrated utterance–parse entailment.

That keeps execution and ambiguity detection conceptually distinct. The backbone produces a single output for execution. The ambiguity flag has a stricter condition: it is not triggered just because the backbone is uncertain, but only when alternative parses satisfy the grammar constraint, remain stable under paraphrasing, and pass calibrated utterance–parse entailment.
Why keep the execution backbone single-output if the point is to recognize multiple interpretations?

Recognizing that an utterance admits alternatives does not require changing the execution backbone into a multiple-output executor. In this proposal, the backbone retains its single-output role, while the ambiguity flag indicates when qualifying alternatives are present. That separation is consistent with the goal of preserving performance on unambiguous execution inputs, though the proposal itself does not establish that the performance target has been met.
I want to be precise about “flag ambiguity only when.” Is uncertainty from the backbone ever enough by itself?

No. Under this proposal, uncertainty by itself is not sufficient to raise the ambiguity flag. The flag depends on alternatives that meet the specified checks. The point is to avoid treating difficulty choosing a parse—particularly under an unseen compositional structure—as proof that the utterance genuinely supports more than one interpretation.
What work does “grammar-constrained” do in that condition?

It limits the alternatives considered for the flag to parses that satisfy the grammar constraint. A candidate does not qualify merely because a model can suggest it. At the same time, grammatical admissibility alone is not enough: the proposal also requires paraphrase stability and calibrated utterance–parse entailment.
And “paraphrase-stable” means the alternative should not depend on a fragile wording accident?

That is the intended conceptual role. An alternative treated as evidence of ambiguity should remain supported across paraphrasings, rather than appearing only because of an unstable response to one wording. The proposal does not specify how paraphrases are obtained, how stability is measured, or a numerical stability cutoff.
Could a parse be grammar-constrained and paraphrase-stable yet still fail the condition?

Yes. It must also pass calibrated utterance–parse entailment. The three qualifications are not substitutes for one another: a grammar-compliant parse that behaves consistently under paraphrasing still should not trigger the flag unless the utterance supports that parse under the calibrated entailment check.
Please unpack “utterance–parse entailment” without assuming an implementation.

It asks whether the utterance supports the proposed parse as an interpretation, rather than merely whether the parse is structurally permissible or was produced confidently. The word “calibrated” makes that support check part of the proposed decision condition, but the node does not prescribe a particular entailment model, calibration procedure, or threshold.
So calibration does not give us a stated numerical cutoff here?

Right. The proposal says alternatives must pass calibrated utterance–parse entailment; it does not supply a cutoff or say how calibration is carried out. It would be premature to turn that phrase into a specific numerical rule.
Suppose the backbone has a low-confidence single output, and no alternative passes all three checks. What would the proposal say about the flag?

It would not raise the ambiguity flag on that basis. Low confidence could still signal that the backbone is uncertain, but the proposed condition for flagging ambiguity has not been met. That is exactly why the proposal separates model uncertainty from evidence for genuinely valid alternatives.
What if an alternative passes the grammar constraint but not the paraphrase-stability condition?

Then it does not satisfy the stated condition for flagging ambiguity. Being grammar-constrained is necessary within this proposal, but it is not sufficient. The alternative must also be paraphrase-stable and pass calibrated utterance–parse entailment.
What if it passes the entailment check but violates the grammar constraint?
It likewise would not qualify under the proposal. The ambiguity flag is reserved for alternatives that satisfy the combined condition, not for alternatives that satisfy only one of its parts.
Does “alternatives” mean the backbone stops choosing a single output for execution when the flag is raised?

No such change is specified. The design explicitly keeps a single-output execution backbone. The ambiguity flag communicates that qualifying alternatives exist; it does not, by itself, redefine how the backbone’s execution output is selected or used.
I also do not want the checks described as if they guarantee that every flagged utterance is truly ambiguous.

Agreed. This is a proposal for when to raise the flag, not a claim of perfect detection. Whether it distinguishes genuine ambiguity from uncertainty well enough would need to be assessed against independently annotated sets of valid interpretations, including on unseen compositions. No such result is stated here.
How does this proposal relate to the F1 ≥0.85 requirement?

It offers a decision rule intended to support that goal, not evidence that the threshold has been reached. The requirement remains ambiguity-detection F1 ≥0.85 on unseen compositions, using independently annotated sets of valid interpretations. The proposed checks describe what would have to qualify before the parser raises its ambiguity flag.
And the comparison with a single-output parser trained on identical data?

Retaining a single-output execution backbone aligns the proposal with that comparison: on unambiguous inputs, execution accuracy is meant to match that of a single-output parser trained on identical data. Keeping the backbone single-output does not itself prove an accuracy match; the comparison remains a separate requirement.
Can I say that paraphrase stability proves the utterance has multiple valid interpretations?

No. Paraphrase stability is one proposed check on an alternative, not a proof by itself. The alternative must also be grammar-constrained and pass calibrated utterance–parse entailment, and genuine ambiguity is ultimately distinct from the parser’s own behavior under paraphrasing.
I want the distinction between an alternative parse and an uncertain prediction to stay prominent.

An uncertain prediction describes the model’s state about what to output. A qualifying alternative, in this proposal, is a candidate interpretation that meets the grammar constraint, remains stable under paraphrasing, and passes calibrated entailment from the utterance. The ambiguity flag is tied to the latter, not merely to uncertainty about the backbone’s single output.
Would it be accurate to describe the proposal as three filters applied to alternatives plus a separate execution path?

As a conceptual description, yes: alternatives must satisfy grammar constraints, paraphrase stability, and calibrated utterance–parse entailment before they can support an ambiguity flag, while execution retains a single-output backbone. “Filters” should not be taken to imply a specified ordering or implementation, because neither is given.
Then give me the design in one sentence, keeping it clearly a proposal.

The proposal is to retain a single-output execution backbone and flag ambiguity only when alternative parses are grammar-constrained, paraphrase-stable, and pass calibrated utterance–parse entailment, rather than treating model uncertainty alone as ambiguity.
What entailment and paraphrase-consistency thresholds would reject beam-search artifacts without discarding valid alternative parses on unseen compositions?

There are no numerical thresholds specified yet. That is the open question: where to place the calibrated utterance–parse entailment and paraphrase-consistency cutoffs so a candidate produced by beam search is not mistaken for a valid alternative, while genuine alternatives remain eligible for the ambiguity flag on unseen compositions.
Why not just require very high scores on both checks?

A very strict requirement could reject artifacts, but it could also discard valid alternative parses. The threshold question has two sides: excluding candidates that lack sufficient support and retaining interpretations that are genuinely valid, including when the compositional structure is unseen. Higher cutoffs are not automatically better.
And if the cutoffs are too permissive?

Then beam-search candidates that do not represent valid interpretations may pass the checks and be treated as evidence of ambiguity. A candidate’s presence in the beam is not, by itself, evidence that the utterance supports it.
What exactly does the entailment threshold decide?

It decides how much calibrated utterance–parse support is required before an alternative can contribute to the ambiguity flag. The question is not whether the candidate is a possible parser output, but whether the utterance supports that parse as a valid interpretation. The specific score scale and cutoff are not given.
What is the separate role of the paraphrase-consistency threshold?

It sets how stable the alternative must be under paraphrasing to qualify. That is a distinct check from utterance–parse entailment: a candidate might appear well supported for one wording yet fail to remain stable, or it might appear stable without being sufficiently supported as an interpretation. Neither check should be silently substituted for the other.
Could I take the highest-scoring beam alternative and flag ambiguity whenever its entailment score clears the cutoff?

Not under the stated proposal. An alternative must also be grammar-constrained and paraphrase-stable. More importantly, this question asks how to set the entailment and consistency thresholds so beam-search artifacts are rejected without losing valid alternatives; being highest-scoring within a beam does not settle whether a candidate is valid.
Is there a known entailment value that cleanly separates artifacts from valid parses?

None is supplied. It would be unwarranted to name a value or claim a clean separation. The open issue is precisely whether and where calibrated thresholds can make that distinction while preserving valid alternative parses on unseen compositions.
Could the paraphrase-consistency threshold be set without considering which paraphrases are involved?

The meaning of consistency depends on what is being compared. In particular, a wording that changes the interpretation available from the utterance should not automatically be treated the same as one that preserves it. The question does not specify a paraphrase set, a consistency measure, or a cutoff, so it does not support a concrete numerical answer.
I worry that demanding consistency might erase real ambiguity. Is that part of the threshold problem?

Yes. If the consistency requirement is too strict, a valid alternative could be discarded rather than recognized. The aim is to use paraphrase stability to screen out fragile candidates without making stability so demanding that it becomes incompatible with retaining genuine alternatives.
But a low consistency cutoff might let beam artifacts through even if entailment is calibrated?

It might. Calibration of the entailment check does not make the paraphrase-consistency choice irrelevant. The question concerns their combined ability to reject artifacts while retaining valid parses; neither threshold can be judged solely by how many candidates it admits.
Does passing both thresholds prove that a candidate is valid?

It would mean the candidate passes the proposed checks, not that validity has been proved. The thresholds are intended to make the ambiguity decision more discriminating. Whether they succeed, especially on unseen compositions, must be judged against independently annotated sets of valid interpretations rather than inferred from the scores alone.
So I should not describe every candidate the beam produces as an alternative interpretation?

Right. A beam-search candidate can be considered for the checks, but appearing in the beam does not make it a valid alternative interpretation. The open threshold question is about separating such artifacts from genuinely valid alternatives without discarding the latter.
How does this connect to distinguishing utterance ambiguity from model uncertainty?

A model can be uncertain and produce competing candidates even when the utterance has only one valid interpretation. Requiring alternatives to clear the entailment and paraphrase-consistency checks is meant to prevent that uncertainty from automatically becoming an ambiguity flag. The thresholds have to be chosen carefully, though, or the checks could also suppress genuine ambiguity.
Could one threshold compensate for a failure on the other?

The proposal says alternatives should be paraphrase-stable and pass calibrated utterance–parse entailment. It does not specify a compensating score or an exception where strength on one check makes failure on the other acceptable. The present question is about appropriate thresholds for both checks, not a stated trade-off rule between them.
Should I expect the same cutoff to work on unseen compositions as on familiar ones?

That cannot be concluded from the information given. The question explicitly focuses on unseen compositions, so the crucial issue is whether the chosen thresholds reject artifacts and retain valid alternatives there. A cutoff’s behavior in another setting would not establish that on its own.
If I discuss evaluation, what evidence is relevant without pretending we have results?

The independently annotated sets of valid interpretations provide the reference for deciding whether alternatives are genuine. They can be used to assess the consequences of candidate thresholds on unseen compositions: artifacts incorrectly admitted and valid alternatives incorrectly discarded. That describes what would need checking, not an outcome or a selected threshold.
And the ambiguity-detection F1 ≥0.85 target does not tell me the entailment cutoff numerically?

Correct. F1 ≥0.85 is a performance target for ambiguity detection on unseen compositions, not an entailment or paraphrase-consistency cutoff. Different cutoff choices could affect whether that target is reached, but the target alone does not determine either threshold.
Does retaining the single-output execution backbone resolve this threshold question?

No. Keeping the execution backbone single-output preserves the proposed separation between execution and the ambiguity flag. It does not specify how much entailment support or paraphrase consistency an alternative must show before that flag is raised.
Then what is the most faithful short answer to my original question?

The thresholds remain undetermined. They need to be calibrated so grammar-constrained alternatives that are merely beam-search artifacts fail the entailment or paraphrase-consistency checks, while genuinely valid alternative parses on unseen compositions are retained; no particular numeric cutoffs or demonstrated balance are stated.

Here is a threshold hypothesis: requiring utterance–parse entailment ≥0.80 and agreement across three of four paraphrases will yield ambiguity-detection F1 ≥0.85 without reducing unambiguous execution accuracy.

That is a testable hypothesis, not an observed result. It proposes two conditions for qualifying alternatives—entailment of at least 0.80 and agreement across three of four paraphrases—and predicts two outcomes: ambiguity-detection F1 of at least 0.85 and no reduction in execution accuracy on unambiguous inputs.
Does this answer the question about thresholds for beam-search artifacts?

It proposes an answer. The idea is that those cutoffs may reject beam-search artifacts while retaining valid alternative parses. The hypothesis does not establish that they do so, particularly on unseen compositions; that remains to be assessed.
I want to avoid making 0.80 sound like a measured boundary between valid parses and artifacts.

Then describe ≥0.80 as the proposed entailment requirement. Nothing here shows that 0.80 is a natural separation point, an optimized value, or a threshold that has already produced the predicted F1. Its effectiveness is what the hypothesis puts in question.
Is the inequality important? Would a score of exactly 0.80 qualify under this wording?

Yes. The symbol ≥ makes the proposed entailment condition inclusive: a score of exactly 0.80 meets it. That says only that the candidate clears this particular proposed requirement, not that it automatically qualifies as a valid alternative.
How should I phrase the paraphrase part so I preserve the count?

Say “agreement across three of four paraphrases.” That retains both numbers and the intended consistency condition. The hypothesis does not define the agreement measure or how the four paraphrases are obtained, so it is best not to add either detail.
Would agreement across all four also satisfy a three-of-four requirement?

On the ordinary reading of “requiring agreement across three of four,” yes: agreement across four would meet a requirement of at least three. The important distinction is that the hypothesis does not demand agreement across every one of the four paraphrases.
Does a candidate that meets the entailment requirement but agrees across only two paraphrases pass?

No. It would miss the proposed three-of-four agreement requirement. The hypothesis combines the entailment and paraphrase-consistency conditions; clearing one does not remove the need to clear the other.
What about agreement across three paraphrases with entailment below 0.80?
That would miss the proposed entailment requirement. The candidate would need both entailment ≥0.80 and the specified paraphrase agreement to pass these two checks.
Should I still mention the grammar constraint from the parser proposal?

Yes, if you are describing where the thresholds fit. The proposal considers grammar-constrained alternatives and flags ambiguity only when qualifying alternatives pass the additional checks. This hypothesis supplies candidate values for the entailment and paraphrase-consistency checks; it does not replace the grammar constraint.
Is passing those checks the same as proving that an utterance is genuinely ambiguous?

No. Passing the proposed checks would support raising an ambiguity flag under the proposed design, but it would not itself prove that multiple interpretations are valid. The independently annotated sets of valid interpretations remain the reference for assessing whether the flag reflects genuine utterance ambiguity rather than model uncertainty.
What exactly is the predicted F1 outcome?

The prediction is ambiguity-detection F1 ≥0.85. In the stated goal, that target applies on unseen compositions using independently annotated sets of valid interpretations. The hypothesis predicts reaching that target with the proposed thresholds; it does not report an achieved score.
Could someone mistakenly read the 0.80 as the expected F1?

Yes, so it helps to keep the quantities distinct. ≥0.80 is the proposed utterance–parse entailment cutoff for alternatives. ≥0.85 is the predicted ambiguity-detection F1 outcome. They measure different things and neither number should be substituted for the other.
And the three-of-four figure is not a percentage of ambiguous utterances detected?
Correct. It describes the proposed agreement condition across four paraphrases for an alternative. It is not the ambiguity-detection F1, and it does not state a detection rate across utterances.
I also want the execution-accuracy part stated carefully.

The hypothesis predicts that applying these requirements will not reduce execution accuracy on unambiguous inputs. That is a predicted preservation of accuracy, not a measured finding. The broader goal separately calls for matching the unambiguous-input execution accuracy of a single-output parser trained on identical data.
Does keeping the single-output backbone guarantee no reduction?

No. Retaining that backbone is part of the proposal, while “without reducing unambiguous execution accuracy” is part of this hypothesis’s predicted outcome. The architectural separation alone does not establish the accuracy result.
Could stricter thresholds help with artifacts but hurt the F1 prediction?

Conceptually, yes: rejecting more candidates could also exclude valid alternative parses, which would work against detecting genuine ambiguity. That is why the hypothesis concerns the balance achieved by these particular requirements, rather than asserting that stricter checks always improve performance. No effect has been measured here.
And looser thresholds could let model uncertainty masquerade as ambiguity?

That is the concern motivating the threshold question. If unsupported beam-search alternatives are admitted, their presence could be mistaken for genuine ambiguity. The proposed entailment and paraphrase-agreement requirements are hypothesized to avoid that problem without discarding too many valid alternatives; their success is not yet established.
Can we say which of the two proposed requirements is more important?

Not from this hypothesis. It states a joint requirement and a predicted outcome, but gives no evidence separating the effect of the ≥0.80 entailment condition from the effect of agreement across three of four paraphrases.
Does the hypothesis specify how to calibrate entailment or select the paraphrases?

No. It specifies the proposed entailment value and paraphrase-agreement count, but not a calibration procedure, paraphrase-selection method, or agreement metric. Those details should not be presented as decisions already contained in the hypothesis.
What is the clearest one-sentence version, with the uncertainty intact?

The hypothesis is that requiring utterance–parse entailment ≥0.80 and agreement across three of four paraphrases for qualifying alternatives will yield ambiguity-detection F1 ≥0.85 on unseen compositions without reducing execution accuracy on unambiguous inputs; neither outcome has been established here.

To address the threshold question, I want to independently annotate sets of valid parses for unseen-composition CompoAmbig-1, then sweep the entailment and paraphrase-consistency thresholds. I would compare ambiguity F1 and unambiguous execution against the single-output baseline.

That is a plan for evaluating threshold choices, not a result. The independently annotated valid-parse sets would provide a reference for genuine ambiguity on unseen-composition CompoAmbig-1. The threshold sweep would then let you compare ambiguity-detection F1 while also checking unambiguous execution against the single-output baseline.
Why do the annotations need to be independent?

The reference sets need to identify which parses are valid without simply accepting the parser’s own candidates or confidence as the answer. Otherwise, a beam-search candidate could appear to validate itself. Independent annotation keeps the assessment of utterance ambiguity separate from model uncertainty.
Am I committing to a particular number of annotators or an annotation procedure?
No. The plan says to independently annotate valid-parse sets for unseen-composition CompoAmbig-1. It does not specify an annotator count, an adjudication procedure, or other annotation mechanics.
Why sets of valid parses rather than one preferred parse per utterance?

A single preferred parse would not, by itself, identify all the interpretations judged valid. Sets of valid parses can serve as the reference for deciding whether an utterance genuinely admits alternatives, which is the distinction the ambiguity flag is meant to capture.
Does the plan assume that every utterance in CompoAmbig-1 is ambiguous?

No. It calls for valid-parse sets for unseen-composition CompoAmbig-1; it does not say every utterance has multiple valid parses. The sets provide the reference needed to distinguish cases with valid alternatives from those without them.
What does sweeping the thresholds add beyond checking one proposed pair of values?

A sweep compares how ambiguity detection and unambiguous execution behave under different threshold choices. That directly addresses the question of where the entailment and paraphrase-consistency requirements should sit: a single pair cannot show how the balance changes as the cutoffs change. The plan does not specify a sweep range, increments, or a chosen pair.
Are these specifically the entailment and paraphrase-consistency thresholds we were discussing?

Yes. They are the thresholds governing when an alternative passes the utterance–parse entailment and paraphrase-consistency checks. Sweeping them is meant to examine whether the checks reject beam-search artifacts without discarding valid alternative parses on unseen compositions.
Does sweeping mean I have already selected the best thresholds?

No. The sweep is planned; no measurements, selection rule, or selected thresholds are stated. It is a way to compare candidate settings against the annotated valid-parse sets and the execution baseline.
How do the valid-parse sets help with the beam-search-artifact concern?

They give an independent reference for whether a proposed alternative is actually valid. That makes it possible to assess whether a threshold setting admits candidates that are merely beam-search artifacts or excludes parses that belong in the valid set. The plan does not yet say how often either error occurs.
I want to keep the two comparisons in the sweep clear. What is ambiguity F1 compared with?

Ambiguity-detection F1 is assessed using the independently annotated sets of valid parses for unseen-composition CompoAmbig-1. Those sets supply the reference for genuine ambiguity; the F1 measure concerns how well the parser detects it. The plan does not report an F1 value.
And what is the unambiguous execution comparison?

It compares execution on unambiguous inputs with the single-output baseline. In the stated goal, that baseline is a single-output parser trained on identical data. The plan calls for making the comparison, not for assuming that execution accuracy already matches it.
Could I report a threshold setting based only on ambiguity F1 and leave execution out?

That would leave out an explicit part of this plan. The sweep calls for comparing both ambiguity F1 and unambiguous execution against the single-output baseline. A setting’s ambiguity result alone would not address the planned execution comparison.
Does the plan say to optimize a combined score for those two measures?
No. It says to compare ambiguity F1 and unambiguous execution while sweeping thresholds. It does not prescribe a combined score, weighting, or threshold-selection rule.
Should I describe CompoAmbig-1 as a benchmark with a known size or existing labels?

No such details are supplied. The plan identifies unseen-composition CompoAmbig-1 as the material for which valid-parse sets will be independently annotated. It does not state its size or say that those annotations already exist.
How does the F1 ≥0.85 goal fit without turning the plan into a success claim?

You can describe ambiguity-detection F1 ≥0.85 on unseen compositions as the goal against which results would matter. The plan is to annotate and sweep thresholds so that F1 can be compared; it does not say the target has been reached.
Likewise, the baseline comparison should not be phrased as if accuracy has already been preserved?
Exactly. The plan is to compare unambiguous execution with the single-output baseline. Whether any threshold setting matches that baseline is not reported here.
Does this plan specify how grammar-constrained alternatives are generated?

No. Grammar-constrained alternatives are part of the parser proposal, but this plan specifies the independent valid-parse annotation and the threshold sweep with its two comparisons. It does not add a candidate-generation procedure.
Can you state the plan concisely while retaining its name and both evaluation measures?

Independently annotate valid-parse sets for unseen-composition CompoAmbig-1, then sweep entailment and paraphrase-consistency thresholds, comparing ambiguity-detection F1 against those annotations and unambiguous execution against the single-output baseline.

The activity is to sweep the entailment and paraphrase thresholds around 0.80 and three-of-four on CompoAmbig-1, then compare ambiguity F1 and unambiguous execution against the single-output baseline.

That makes the proposed threshold pair the center of a comparison rather than treating it as an established answer. The sweep concerns the entailment requirement near 0.80 and the paraphrase-agreement requirement near three of four on CompoAmbig-1. It should show how ambiguity F1 varies while unambiguous execution is compared with the single-output baseline; no outcome is stated yet.
When I say “around 0.80 and three-of-four,” am I saying that both thresholds will vary?

Yes. The activity calls for a sweep of both the entailment and paraphrase thresholds around those proposed values. It does not specify the exact settings to test, their spacing, or how many settings the sweep contains.
The paraphrase condition is a count, whereas entailment has a numerical score. Does it still make sense to call both thresholds?

Yes. The entailment threshold is a required score, with 0.80 as the proposed reference point. The paraphrase threshold is the required level of agreement across four paraphrases, with three-of-four as its reference point. They have different forms, but both determine whether an alternative clears a check.
Should the sweep be described as a test of the claim about F1 ≥0.85?

It evaluates that prediction, along with the prediction that unambiguous execution accuracy will not be reduced. The activity is the threshold sweep and comparison, not a finding that either prediction holds. Ambiguity F1 ≥0.85 remains the target for unseen compositions, not a score already obtained on CompoAmbig-1.
What is the reference for ambiguity F1 in this activity?

The plan calls for independently annotated sets of valid parses for unseen-composition CompoAmbig-1. Those sets provide the reference for whether an utterance admits valid alternative interpretations. The activity does not report annotations or an F1 result as already completed.
And the single-output baseline is not the reference for whether an utterance is ambiguous?

Right. The valid-parse annotations are the reference for ambiguity. The single-output baseline supplies the comparison for execution on unambiguous inputs. Keeping those roles separate avoids treating the baseline’s single prediction as a judgment about every valid interpretation.
What comparison does “unambiguous execution against the single-output baseline” require?

It asks whether execution accuracy on unambiguous inputs matches the single-output parser’s execution accuracy. In the stated goal, that baseline is trained on identical data. The sweep is meant to compare them; it does not state that a match has already been observed.
Would a higher ambiguity F1 automatically make a swept setting preferable?

Not on the basis of this activity alone. Unambiguous execution is also being compared with the single-output baseline. The activity does not prescribe a rule for selecting a setting or for trading a change in execution accuracy against a change in ambiguity F1.
Why examine nearby threshold settings instead of only the exact pair, entailment ≥0.80 and three-of-four agreement?

Examining nearby settings can reveal whether the ambiguity and execution comparisons change as the requirements become more or less restrictive. That is relevant to the concern that a threshold might admit beam-search artifacts or discard valid alternatives. The activity does not assert what those changes will be.
If I tighten the entailment condition, can I say the sweep will remove beam-search artifacts?

No. A stricter entailment requirement may exclude some candidates, but the activity does not establish which excluded candidates would be artifacts or whether valid alternatives would also be lost. The annotated valid-parse sets are needed to assess that distinction.
Likewise, loosening paraphrase agreement might retain more valid parses but also admit artifacts?

That is the possible trade-off the sweep is meant to examine, not an observed result. A less restrictive agreement requirement could admit more alternatives of either kind. Ambiguity F1 against independently annotated valid-parse sets would help assess the resulting ambiguity decisions on CompoAmbig-1.
Is this activity changing the single-output execution backbone?

No change to the backbone is specified. The activity varies the entailment and paraphrase thresholds used for considering alternatives and compares unambiguous execution with the single-output baseline. It should not be described as a new execution architecture.
Does a candidate need to pass only one of the two swept checks?

Under the proposal being evaluated, qualifying alternatives must pass calibrated utterance–parse entailment and meet the paraphrase-stability condition, in addition to being grammar-constrained. The sweep varies the thresholds for the two checks; it does not turn them into an either-or condition.
Does the activity tell us what range around 0.80 to use?
No. “Around 0.80” identifies the reference point, but the activity gives no lower or upper bound, increments, or list of entailment cutoffs. Supplying those would add a decision that is not stated.
And does it specify which paraphrase-agreement counts to include around three-of-four?
